Text:
Rates Hub
Introduction
The proposed Rates Hub is a modern, centralized rates management system designed to 
streamline the process of publishing deposit rates and index rates for various products. It
replaces the current manual, Excel-based process for determining, approving and 
distributing interest rates with branches, managing and uploading financial deposit and 
index rates critical to daily operation. The system will integrate with 3rd party rates 
providers to fetch rates such as 10Y Treasury, 20Y Treasure and other index rates. It will 
allow users to create rates and get it reviewed by approvers, view daily rates, access 
historical data, adjust rates with proper authorization upload updated rates to FIS Rates 
plan. It will provide end points so other applications that can call to get rates as well as 
provide pub/sub model for applications to subscribe to rates. The solution will leverage 
modern software development practices with a scalable backend and an intuitive 
frontend. Eventually, functions of all rates in the bank will be housed in application called 
“Rates Hub”.
Problem Statement
The current process for determining rates and sharing the rates with various teams, 
departments and branches is manual and involves sharing excel sheets. This created 
several risks, including:
• Inefficiency: Manual rate updates and distribution are time-consuming and prone 
to delays. Mistyped or mis-entered values lead to inaccurate deal pricing.
• Lack of Flexibility: The current system deals with promotional rates, relationshipbased pricing and balance-tiered rates manually.
• Operational Inefficiency: Valuable time and resources are spent on a repetitive 
task that could be automated.
2
• Business Impact: Delayed or incorrect FTP rate uploads affect the pricing 
accuracy, potentially resulting in mispriced deals, lost opportunity, and incorrect 
profit calculations.
• Limited Integrations: The FIS Core Banking platform cannot directly access rates, 
requiring manual interventions. Lacks Rates management applications to be 
reached out by other apps to get the rates.
To address these issues, automation is required to ensure timely rates upload, reduce 
manual intervention, and precisely pricing the loans.
Proposed Solutions: Rates Hub
Rates Hub is a web-based, centralized rates management system that addresses the 
above challenges by providing a secure and integrated platform for rates determination, 
approval and distribution. The system will serve two primary user groups and other 
functions systems.
• Rates committee members: Login to a secured portal to set and approve rates for 
various bank products, Define promotional rates, relationship-based rates and 
balance-tiered rates. Approve and publish rates for distribution.
• Branch Bankers: Login to view daily rate cards tailored to their branch and 
market/region, access real-time rates of offer products to customers accurately 
and efficiently
• Other Applications: Call Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) endpoints by any 
software applications that need rates in real time.
Proposed Technology Stack
• Backend:
o .NET 8 – A robust, enterprise-grade framework with strong API integration 
capabilities, ideal choice as existing Rates app (developed by FinTech 
Advantage) is using same tech. This new IRMS can be incorporated as a new
functionality
o Database – PostgreSQL, an open-source, reliable and supports time-series 
data efficiently, or whatever Database is used by Rates app.
• Frontend:
o React – A popular component-based library for building dynamic UIs.
o Or Angular - a full-fledged framework with built in tools for enterprise 
applications. (React is preferred as it is already used in Rates app)
3
• API Integration:
o FIS Core platform integration via MuleSoft,
o Provide endpoints for any system that needs rates in real time,
o And get any 3rd party integrated via MuleSoft to SNV systems
• Authentication: OAuth 2.0 or JWT for role-based access control, for example, view 
only, versus edit privileges.
• Deployment: Docker containers on Azure for scalability.
System Architecture
1. Backend:
a. Restful API endpoints to handle retrieval, storage, and uploads
b. Scheduled task, for example, .NET worker service to automate daily tasks
c. Database schema for rates, for example, timestamp, rate type, value,
adjusted value, user ID, audit log
d. Service layer for business logic, for example, validation authorization
2. Frontend:
a. Dashboard for daily rates with filters, for example, date range, rate type, etc.
b. Historical data view with charts, for example, using chart.js, highcharts or 
rechart (react chart library)
c. Web Form for rate adjustment with role-based access controls
d. Export functionality for FIS rates plan via MuleSoft API
3. Integration Layer:
a. Communication to any 3rd party vis MuleSoft
b. Provide URI endpoints to any application that needs rates
Key
######################

Rates Hub
Introduction
The proposed Rates Hub is a modern, centralized rates management system designed to 
streamline the process of publishing deposit rates and index rates for various products. It
replaces the current manual, Excel-based process for determining, approving and 
distributing interest rates with branches, managing and uploading financial deposit and 
index rates critical to daily operation. The system will integrate with 3rd party rates 
providers to fetch rates such as 10Y Treasury, 20Y Treasure and other index rates. It will 
allow users to create rates and get it reviewed by approvers, view daily rates, access 
historical data, adjust rates with proper authorization upload updated rates to FIS Rates 
plan. It will provide end points so other applications that can call to get rates as well as 
provide pub/sub model for applications to subscribe to rates. The solution will leverage 
modern software development practices with a scalable backend and an intuitive 
frontend. Eventually, functions of all rates in the bank will be housed in application called 
“Rates Hub”.
Problem Statement
The current process for determining rates and sharing the rates with various teams, 
departments and branches is manual and involves sharing excel sheets. This created 
several risks, including:
• Inefficiency: Manual rate updates and distribution are time-consuming and prone 
to delays. Mistyped or mis-entered values lead to inaccurate deal pricing.
• Lack of Flexibility: The current system deals with promotional rates, relationshipbased pricing and balance-tiered rates manually.
• Operational Inefficiency: Valuable time and resources are spent on a repetitive 
task that could be automated.
2
• Business Impact: Delayed or incorrect FTP rate uploads affect the pricing 
accuracy, potentially resulting in mispriced deals, lost opportunity, and incorrect 
profit calculations.
• Limited Integrations: The FIS Core Banking platform cannot directly access rates, 
requiring manual interventions. Lacks Rates management applications to be 
reached out by other apps to get the rates.
To address these issues, automation is required to ensure timely rates upload, reduce 
manual intervention, and precisely pricing the loans.
Proposed Solutions: Rates Hub
Rates Hub is a web-based, centralized rates management system that addresses the 
above challenges by providing a secure and integrated platform for rates determination, 
approval and distribution. The system will serve two primary user groups and other 
functions systems.
• Rates committee members: Login to a secured portal to set and approve rates for 
various bank products, Define promotional rates, relationship-based rates and 
balance-tiered rates. Approve and publish rates for distribution.
• Branch Bankers: Login to view daily rate cards tailored to their branch and 
market/region, access real-time rates of offer products to customers accurately 
and efficiently
• Other Applications: Call Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) endpoints by any 
software applications that need rates in real time.
Proposed Technology Stack
• Backend:
o .NET 8 – A robust, enterprise-grade framework with strong API integration 
capabilities, ideal choice as existing Rates app (developed by FinTech 
Advantage) is using same tech. This new IRMS can be incorporated as a new
functionality
o Database – PostgreSQL, an open-source, reliable and supports time-series 
data efficiently, or whatever Database is used by Rates app.
• Frontend:
o React – A popular component-based library for building dynamic UIs.
o Or Angular - a full-fledged framework with built in tools for enterprise 
applications. (React is preferred as it is already used in Rates app)
3
• API Integration:
o FIS Core platform integration via MuleSoft,
o Provide endpoints for any system that needs rates in real time,
o And get any 3rd party integrated via MuleSoft to SNV systems
• Authentication: OAuth 2.0 or JWT for role-based access control, for example, view 
only, versus edit privileges.
• Deployment: Docker containers on Azure for scalability.
System Architecture
1. Backend:
a. Restful API endpoints to handle retrieval, storage, and uploads
b. Scheduled task, for example, .NET worker service to automate daily tasks
c. Database schema for rates, for example, timestamp, rate type, value,
adjusted value, user ID, audit log
d. Service layer for business logic, for example, validation authorization
2. Frontend:
a. Dashboard for daily rates with filters, for example, date range, rate type, etc.
b. Historical data view with charts, for example, using chart.js, highcharts or 
rechart (react chart library)
c. Web Form for rate adjustment with role-based access controls
d. Export functionality for FIS rates plan via MuleSoft API
3. Integration Layer:
a. Communication to any 3rd party vis MuleSoft
b. Provide URI endpoints to any application that needs rates
Key

Text:
DD).
Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF)
WSJF is a prioritization model used to sequence jobs (e.g., Features, Capabilities, Epics) based 
on the cost of delay (CoD) and the duration it takes to complete them. It helps Agile teams and 
organizations deliver the maximum economic benefit in the shortest possible time.
It is calculated using the following formula:
WSJF = Cost of Delay / Job Duration
Where:
o Cost of Delay (CoD) = User/Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction and/or 
Opportunity Enablement
o Job Duration = Estimated size or effort (e.g., in story points or team weeks)
Breakdown of WSJF Components
1. User/Business Value
a. How much value the job delivers to the customer or business
b. Often scored on a relative scale (e.g., Fibonacci 1,2,3,5,8,13,21,…)
2. Time Criticality
a. How important it is to deliver the job soon (e.g., regulatory deadline, market window)
3. Risk Reduction / Opportunity Enablement
a. Will this job reduce future risk or enable new business opportunities?
Together, these three form the numerator: Cost of Delay
4. Job Size (Duration)
a. Estimate of the effort required to complete the work
b. Should be consistent across jobs (e.g., story points, team weeks)
c. Smaller jobs generally get a higher WSJF (other factors equal)
Normalized Story Points Definition
Normalized Story Points are a relative estimation technique used by Agile teams to size 
user stories based on effort, complexity, and risk — standardized across teams using a 
shared baseline. When using the Fibonacci sequence and defining 1 Story Point = 1 ideal 
day, the scale provides a structured way to estimate work based on increasing uncertainty.
Effort Mapping (1 SP = 1 Day)
Story Points Equivalent Effort Typical Use Case
1 1 Day Very simple task, trivial logic
2 2 Days Straightforward story with low risk

• What is Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)?
o Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) is an Agile software development practice 
that emphasizes collaboration between business stakeholders, developers, and 
testers to define the expected behavior of a system using concrete examples in 
plain language.
o BDD extends Test-Driven Development (TDD) by shifting the focus from testing 
implementation to specifying behavior, ensuring alignment between technical 
teams and business needs.
• Core Concepts of BDD
o Ubiquitous Language
▪ A common vocabulary used by developers, testers, and business analysts.
▪ Based on the domain model and used consistently in requirements, code, 
and tests.
o Examples and Scenarios
▪ Behavior is described through concrete, real-world examples.
▪ These examples are formatted into structured scenarios using Gherkin 
syntax.
o Executable Specifications
▪ The behavior examples become automated tests.
▪ They serve as both documentation and regression tests.
BDD Process (End-to-End)
1. Discovery – Understand Desired Behavior
a. Conducted as a collaborative discussion (often called a “Three Amigos” meeting).
b. Participants: Product Owner (or BA), Developer, Tester.
c. Goal: Clarify requirements and uncover edge cases.
d. Output: Shared understanding + candidate scenarios.
2. Formulation – Write Scenarios
a. Scenarios are expressed in Gherkin syntax, which uses:
Feature: <high-level capability>
Scenario: <specific case>
Given <precondition>
When <action or event>
Then <expected outcome>
3. Automation – Make It Executable
a. The Given/When/Then steps are mapped to code functions using BDD tools.
b. Each step is tied to actual system behavior (methods or service calls).
c. Tools parse the Gherkin file and execute the mapped step definitions.
4. Development – Write Code to Pass Scenarios
a. Developers implement just enough code to make the scenario pass.
b. Tests drive the design of the system by focusing on desired behavior
5. Validation and Continuous Integration
a. BDD scenarios are integrated into the CI/CD pipeline.

Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF)
WSJF is a prioritization model used to sequence jobs (e.g., Features, Capabilities, Epics) based 
on the cost of delay (CoD) and the duration it takes to complete them. It helps Agile teams and 
organizations deliver the maximum economic benefit in the shortest possible time.
It is calculated using the following formula:
WSJF = Cost of Delay / Job Duration
Where:
o Cost of Delay (CoD) = User/Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction and/or 
Opportunity Enablement
o Job Duration = Estimated size or effort (e.g., in story points or team weeks)
Breakdown of WSJF Components
1. User/Business Value
a. How much value the job delivers to the customer or business
b. Often scored on a relative scale (e.g., Fibonacci 1,2,3,5,8,13,21,…)
2. Time Criticality
a. How important it is to deliver the job soon (e.g., regulatory deadline, market window)
3. Risk Reduction / Opportunity Enablement
a. Will this job reduce future risk or enable new business opportunities?
Together, these three form the numerator: Cost of Delay
4. Job Size (Duration)
a. Estimate of the effort required to complete the work
b. Should be consistent across jobs (e.g., story points, team weeks)
c. Smaller jobs generally get a higher WSJF (other factors equal)
Normalized Story Points Definition
Normalized Story Points are a relative estimation technique used by Agile teams to size 
user stories based on effort, complexity, and risk — standardized across teams using a 
shared baseline. When using the Fibonacci sequence and defining 1 Story Point = 1 ideal 
day, the scale provides a structured way to estimate work based on increasing uncertainty.
Effort Mapping (1 SP = 1 Day)
Story Points Equivalent Effort Typical Use Case
1 1 Day Very simple task, trivial logic
2 2 Days Straightforward story with low risk
3 3 Days Moderate complexity, no major unknowns
5 5 Days (1 Week) More complex, may involve integration or testing
8 8 days (2 Weeks) Cross-functional, may include edge cases or rework

V – Valuable
o The story must clearly explain who benefits and how.
o Helps Product Owners prioritize work by ROI.
o Even technical stories should map to business value (e.g., improving performance,

o Tip: Use the format:
o “As a [role], I want [story] so that [benefit].”
E – Estimable
o The team must have enough information to size the story.
o If not, it may need spikes, prototypes, or clarification.
o Estimation helps with capacity planning and velocity tracking.
o Tip: If you can't estimate it, you probably don’t understand it well enough yet.
S – Small
o Stories should be small enough to fit into a single sprint.
o If too large, break into vertical slices (e.g., UI + backend + integration for one use 
case).
o Tip: A typical story should take 1–3 days of effort. If it's longer, split it while

T – Testable
o There must be clear acceptance criteria.

o Ideally written using Given/When/Then or a checklist.
o Tip: If it can’t be tested, it can’t be considered done.
Behavior Driven Development (BDD)
• What is Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)?
o Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) is an Agile software development practice 
that emphasizes collaboration between business stakeholders, developers, and 
testers to define the expected behavior of a system using concrete examples in 
plain language.
o BDD extends Test-Driven Development (TDD) by shifting the focus from testing 
implementation to specifying behavior, ensuring alignment between technical 
teams and business needs.
• Core Concepts of BDD
o Ubiquitous Language
▪ A common vocabulary used by developers, testers, and business analysts.
▪ Based on the domain model and used consistently in requirements, code, 
and tests.
o Examples and Scenarios
▪ Behavior is described through concrete, real-world examples.
▪ These examples are formatted into structured scenarios using Gherkin 
syntax.
o Executable Specifications
▪ The behavior examples become automated tests.
▪ They serve as both documentation and regression tests.
BDD Process (End-to-End)
1. Discovery – Understand Desired Behavior
a. Conducted as a collaborative discussion (often called a “Three Amigos” meeting).
b. Participants: Product Owner (or BA), Developer, Tester.
c. Goal: Clarify requirements and uncover edge cases.
d. Output: Shared understanding + candidate scenarios.
2. Formulation – Write Scenarios
a. Scenarios are expressed in Gherkin syntax, which uses:
Feature: <high-level capability>
Scenario: <specific case>
Given <precondition>
When <action or event>
Then <expected outcome>
3. Automation – Make It Executable
a. The Given/When/Then steps are mapped to code functions using BDD tools.
b. Each step is tied to actual system behavior (methods or service calls).
c. Tools parse the Gherkin file and execute the mapped step definitions.
4. Development – Write Code to Pass Scenarios
a. Developers implement just enough code to make the scenario pass.
b. Tests drive the design of the system by focusing on desired behavior
5. Validation and Continuous Integration
a. BDD scenarios are integrated into the CI/CD pipeline.
BDD in SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework)
1. BDD complements Agile Teams, ARTs, and PI Planning by:
2. Supporting Built-In Quality.
3. Ensuring that User Stories and Enablers are validated early.
4. Enhancing Test-First and Continuous Delivery pipelines.
5. Can be tied to Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD).
Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF)
WSJF is a prioritization model used to sequence jobs (e.g., Features, Capabilities, Epics) based 
on the cost of delay (CoD) and the duration it takes to complete them. It helps Agile teams and 
organizations deliver the maximum economic benefit in the shortest possible time.
It is calculated using the following formula:
WSJF = Cost of Delay / Job Duration
Where:
o Cost of Delay (CoD) = User/Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction and/or 
Opportunity Enablement
o Job Duration = Estimated size or effort (e.g., in story points or team weeks)
Breakdown of WSJF Components
1. User/Business Value
a. How much value the job delivers to the customer or business
b. Often scored on a relative scale (e.g., Fibonacci 1,2,3,5,8,13,21,…)
2. Time Criticality

Design Thinking Definition
Design Thinking is a human-centered, iterative problem-solving approach used to 
understand user needs, redefine problems, and create innovative solutions. It emphasizes 
empathy, creativity, and experimentation to solve complex challenges in a user-focused 
way.
Design Thinking integrates the needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and the 
requirements for business success.
Core Principles of Design Thinking
o Human-centered: Focus on real user needs.
o Iterative: Continuously refine ideas and solutions.
o Collaborative: Involves cross-functional teams and stakeholders.
o Experimental: Encourages rapid prototyping and learning from failure.
Design Thinking Process Steps
While there are multiple models, the most commonly used (from Stanford d.school and 
IDEO) includes 5 stages:
1. Empathize
Goal: Understand users, their environment, and their challenges.
o Engage with users through interviews, observation, shadowing.
o Discover emotional drivers, pain points, and hidden needs.
o Avoid assumptions — seek deep empathy.
Tools: User interviews, empathy maps, journey mapping
2. Define
Goal: Clearly articulate the problem to be solved.
o Synthesize insights gathered during empathy.
o Frame the problem as a point of view (POV) statement:
o “[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight].”
Tools: Problem statements, affinity diagrams, “How Might We” questions
3. Ideate 
Goal: Generate a wide range of creative solutions.
o Encourage divergent thinking — quantity over quality first.
o Use brainstorming, mind mapping, or sketching to explore ideas.
o No judgment — build on each other’s ideas.
Tools: Brainstorming, SCAMPER, mind maps
4. Prototype 
Goal: Build low-fidelity versions of ideas to explore and validate them.
o Create rough, fast, inexpensive models of solutions.
o Could be paper sketches, wireframes, mockups, or physical models.
o The aim is to learn, not to perfect.
Tools: Paper prototypes, clickable mockups, 3D models
5. Test 
Goal: Gather feedback from real users to refine the solution.
o Observe users interacting with the prototype.
o Ask open-ended questions, look for pain points or confusion.
o Refine based on feedback — possibly return to earlier steps.
Tools: Usability tests, A/B testing, feedback surveys
Iterative Nature
Design Thinking is non-linear. You may jump between steps:
o Go back to Empathize after a failed test.
o Reframe the Define phase after deeper insights emerge.
o Rapidly prototype and test to validate multiple ideas.
Use Cases of Design Thinking
o Product and service innovation
o Customer experience redesign
o Business model development
o Organizational change initiatives
Persona Definition
A persona is a semi-fictional representation of a specific type of user or customer based on 
real-world data, research, and behavior patterns. Personas help teams understand the 
goals, needs, motivations, pain points, and behaviors of their target audience.
They are commonly used in:
o User experience (UX) design
o Product development
o Marketing
o Agile frameworks (e.g., SAFe, Scrum, Design Thinking)
Key Characteristics of a Persona
Element Description
Name A realistic name that personalizes the profile
Demographics Age, location, job title, income, education, etc.
Goals and Objectives What the persona is trying to achieve
Pain Points Frustrations, blockers, or challenges
Behaviors How they interact with your product or service
Tools/Devices Platforms or devices they commonly use
Quotes or Mindset Key expressions or attitudes that capture their thinking
Example Persona (for a productivity app)
Name: Sarah Martinez
Role: Project Manager
Age: 34
Goals:
o Keep team projects on schedule
o Reduce meeting time
o Improve cross-team visibility
Pain Points:
o Tool overload
o Difficult onboarding for new team members
o Poor integration with reporting systems
Quote:
"I need tools that help my team get work done, not add more work."
Why Personas Matter
o Build empathy with real users
o Drive design and development decisions
o Guide feature prioritization and product roadmaps
o Improve marketing messaging and user onboarding
o Align teams around a shared understanding of the user
Best Practices
o Base personas on qualitative and quantitative research (not assumptions)
o Keep them focused and realistic (avoid generic catch-all personas)
o Use multiple personas if your product serves different user types
o Update personas periodically as you gather more data
Persona Template
Basic Information
o Name: (e.g., Sarah Martinez)
o Photo

Design Thinking Definition
Design Thinking is a human-centered, iterative problem-solving approach used to 
understand user needs, redefine problems, and create innovative solutions. It emphasizes 
empathy, creativity, and experimentation to solve complex challenges in a user-focused 
way.
Design Thinking integrates the needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and the 
requirements for business success.
Core Principles of Design Thinking
o Human-centered: Focus on real user needs.
o Iterative: Continuously refine ideas and solutions.
o Collaborative: Involves cross-functional teams and stakeholders.
o Experimental: Encourages rapid prototyping and learning from failure.
Design Thinking Process Steps
While there are multiple models, the most commonly used (from Stanford d.school and 
IDEO) includes 5 stages:
1. Empathize
Goal: Understand users, their environment, and their challenges.
o Engage with users through interviews, observation, shadowing.
o Discover emotional drivers, pain points, and hidden needs.
o Avoid assumptions — seek deep empathy.
Tools: User interviews, empathy maps, journey mapping
2. Define
Goal: Clearly articulate the problem to be solved.
o Synthesize insights gathered during empathy.
o Frame the problem as a point of view (POV) statement:
o “[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight].”
Tools: Problem statements, affinity diagrams, “How Might We” questions
3. Ideate 
Goal: Generate a wide range of creative solutions.
o Encourage divergent thinking — quantity over quality first.
o Use brainstorming, mind mapping, or sketching to explore ideas.
o No judgment — build on each other’s ideas.
Tools: Brainstorming, SCAMPER, mind maps
4. Prototype 
Goal: Build low-fidelity versions of ideas to explore and validate them.
o Create rough, fast, inexpensive models of solutions.
o Could be paper sketches, wireframes, mockups, or physical models.
o The aim is to learn, not to perfect.
Tools: Paper prototypes, clickable mockups, 3D models
5. Test 
Goal: Gather feedback from real users to refine the solution.
o Observe users interacting with the prototype.
o Ask open-ended questions, look for pain points or confusion.
o Refine based on feedback — possibly return to earlier steps.
Tools: Usability tests, A/B testing, feedback surveys
Iterative Nature
Design Thinking is non-linear. You may jump between steps:
o Go back to Empathize after a failed test.
o Reframe the Define phase after deeper insights emerge.
o Rapidly prototype and test to validate multiple ideas.
Use Cases of Design Thinking
o Product and service innovation
o Customer experience redesign
o Business model development
o Organizational change initiatives
Persona Definition
A persona is a semi-fictional representation of a specific type of user or customer based on 
real-world data, research, and behavior patterns. Personas help teams understand the 
goals, needs, motivations, pain points, and behaviors of their target audience.
They are commonly used in:
o User experience (UX) design
o Product development
o Marketing
o Agile frameworks (e.g., SAFe, Scrum, Design Thinking)
Key Characteristics of a Persona
Element Description
Name A realistic name that personalizes the profile
Demographics Age, location, job title, income, education, etc.
Goals and Objectives What the persona is trying to achieve
Pain Points Frustrations, blockers, or challenges
Behaviors How they interact with your product or service
Tools/Devices Platforms or devices they commonly use
Quotes or Mindset Key expressions or attitudes that capture their thinking

Best Practices

o Use multiple personas if your product serves different user types
o Update personas periodically as you gather more data

### **1. Project Goals and Scope**
The Rates Hub application aims to modernize and centralize the management of financial rates, replacing manual processes with an automated, secure, and user-friendly system. The primary objectives include:
- Streamlining the process of publishing, approving, and distributing deposit and index rates.
- Providing role-based access control for secure and efficient rate management.
- Enabling visualization and reporting of rate changes through dynamic charts and reports.

---

1. **User Roles and Login Functionality**:
   - Implement user authentication and authorization.
   - Define roles such as Viewer, Editor, and Admin with specific permissions.

2. **Role-Based Access Control**:
   - Ensure that only authorized users can perform specific actions, such as adjusting rates or approving changes.

3. **Admin Approval for Rates**:
   - Introduce an approval workflow where rate changes must be reviewed and approved by an Admin before being published.

4. **Reports Page for Changing Rates**:
   - Develop a dedicated page to track and display changes in rates.
   - Include features for filtering and searching rate changes.

5. **Visualization of Rate Data**:
   - Integrate bar charts and other plots to visualize rate trends and historical data.
   - Use libraries like Highcharts or React-based charting tools for dynamic visualizations.

#### **Non-Functional Requirements**
1. **Scalability**:
   - Deploy the application using Docker containers on Azure to ensure scalability and reliability.

2. **Security**:
   - Implement OAuth 2.0 or JWT for secure authentication.
   - Ensure audit logging for all rate changes and user actions.

3. **Integration**:
   - Provide API endpoints for integration with external systems like FIS Core Banking Platform.
   - Enable third-party systems to fetch rates in real-time.

4. **Usability**:
   - Design an intuitive frontend using React for a seamless user experience.

---

### **3. Potential Modules or Components**
1. **Authentication and Authorization Module**:
   - Handles user login, role assignment, and access control.

2. **Rate Management Module**:
   - Allows users to create, adjust, and approve rates.
   - Includes workflows for admin approval.

3. **Reporting and Visualization Module**:
   - Displays rate changes and historical data using charts and reports.

4. **Integration Layer**:
   - Facilitates communication with third-party systems and APIs.

5. **Audit and Logging Module**:
   - Tracks all user actions and rate changes for compliance and troubleshooting.

---

### **4. Dependencies, Risks, and Considerations**
#### **Dependencies**:
- Integration with FIS Core Banking Platform and third-party rate providers.
- Use of libraries like React and Highcharts for frontend development.

#### **Risks**:
- Potential delays in integration with external systems.
- Ensuring data security and compliance with financial regulations.

#### **Considerations**:
- Define clear workflows for rate approval to avoid bottlenecks.
- Ensure the system is tested for scalability and performance under high load.

---

1. **Phase-Wise Development**:
   - Start with core functionalities like user roles, login, and rate management.
   - Gradually add reporting, visualization, and integration features.

2. **Technology Stack**:
   - Use .NET for backend development and React for the frontend.
   - Leverage Docker and Azure for deployment.

3. **Focus on Security**:
   - Implement robust authentication and authorization mechanisms.
   - Ensure all data is encrypted during transmission and storage.

4. **Testing and Validation**:
   - Conduct thorough testing, including unit, integration, and user acceptance testing (UAT).
   - Validate the system against compliance requirements.

5. **User Training and Documentation**:
   - Provide training for Rates Committee Members and other users.
   - Create detailed documentation for system usage and troubleshooting.

To incorporate technical requirements into user story creation, the following guidelines and best practices from the knowledge base can be applied:

---

### User Story Creation Guidelines with Technical Requirements

#### **1. Follow the INVEST Criteria**
Ensure that user stories are:
- **Independent**: Self-contained and not dependent on other stories.
- **Negotiable**: Open for refinement and discussion.
- **Valuable**: Delivering clear business or customer value, even for technical stories.
- **Estimable**: Providing enough clarity for effort estimation.
- **Small**: Sized to fit within a single sprint.
- **Testable**: Including clear acceptance criteria for validation.

#### **2. Include Technical Context**
- Clearly document any **technical enablers** or dependencies required for the story. For example, infrastructure setup, compliance requirements, or architectural considerations.
- Attach relevant **UX mockups, wireframes, or prototypes** if applicable.
- Specify **non-functional requirements** such as performance, security, and scalability constraints.

#### **3. Acceptance Criteria**
- Use **Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)** format for acceptance criteria:
  - **Given**: Precondition or setup.
  - **When**: Action or event.
  - **Then**: Expected outcome.
- Ensure criteria are **testable** and aligned with SAFe's Built-In Quality principles.
- For technical stories, acceptance criteria should validate the technical implementation (e.g., "API response time must be under 200ms").

#### **4. Dependencies and Coordination**
- Identify and address **cross-team or cross-ART dependencies**. Document these dependencies on the Program Board for visibility.
- Coordinate with the **System Architect** or other technical leaders to ensure feasibility and alignment.

#### **5. Traceability and Alignment**
- Link user stories to higher-level **Features** or **Epics** to maintain traceability.
- Ensure stories align with strategic themes and business drivers.

#### **6. Definition of Ready (DoR)**
Before pulling a user story into development, ensure:
- Technical requirements are reviewed and approved by relevant stakeholders (e.g., System Architect, Product Owner).
- Any **blockers** or unresolved risks are addressed.
- The story fits within the team's iteration capacity.

---

### Example User Story Template with Technical Requirements

**Acceptance Criteria**:  
- **Given** the API is deployed in the production environment,  
- **When** a user sends a request,  
- **Then** the response time should be under 200ms.  

**Technical Requirements**:  
- Implement caching mechanisms.  
- Ensure database queries are optimized.  
- Conduct load testing to validate performance under peak traffic.

### **General Guidelines**

   - **Negotiable**: Stories should be placeholders for conversation and refinement during backlog grooming or planning.
   - **Valuable**: Each story must deliver clear business or customer value, even for internal technical tasks.
   - **Estimable**: Provide enough clarity for the team to estimate effort.
   - **Small**: Stories should be small enough to fit within a single sprint.
   - **Testable**: Define clear acceptance criteria to validate completion.

   - Template: “As a [role], I want [activity] so that [business value].”
   - Example: “As an Admin, I want to edit the rates dashboard so that I can update rate trends for the organization.”

3. **Ensure Traceability**:
   - Link each user story to a feature or requirement in the program backlog.
   - Clearly articulate the business value and context for each story.

---

#### **Login Functionality**
- **User Story**: “As a user, I want to log in securely so that I can access my assigned roles and permissions.”
- **Acceptance Criteria**:

  - Given invalid credentials, when the user attempts to log in, then they should see an error message.

- **Acceptance Criteria**:
  - Given an Admin user, when they assign edit permissions, then the selected user should gain access to edit the rates dashboard.
  - Given an Admin user, when they revoke edit permissions, then the selected user should lose access to edit the rates dashboard.

#### **Rates Dashboard**
- **User Story**: “As a Reviewer, I want to view rate trends on the dashboard so that I can analyze rate changes over time.”
- **Acceptance Criteria**:
  - Given a Reviewer, when they access the dashboard, then they should see visualizations for rate trends, comparisons, and historical changes.
  - Given a Reviewer, when they attempt to edit the dashboard, then they should be denied access.

---

### **Workflow Requirements**
#### **Editor Workflow**
- **User Story**: “As an Editor, I want to create or edit rates and send requests to the Reviewer so that rate changes can be reviewed.”
- **Acceptance Criteria**:
  - Given an Editor, when they submit a request, then the Reviewer should receive a notification.

#### **Reviewer Workflow**
- **User Story**: “As a Reviewer, I want to approve or reject rate change requests with comments so that I can provide feedback to the Editor.”
- **Acceptance Criteria**:

  - Given a Reviewer, when they reject a request, then the Editor should receive a notification with comments.

- **Acceptance Criteria**:

### Project Analysis: Rates Hub Functionalities and Requirements

#### 1. **Project Goals and Scope**
The Rates Hub project aims to modernize and centralize the management of deposit and index rates for financial products. - **Login Functionality**: Secure login mechanism for all users.
- **Role-Based Access Control**: Restrict system functionalities based on user roles (Editor, Reviewer, Admin).

- **Editor**:
  - Make edits to rates.
  - Send requests to the Reviewer for approval.

  - Approve or reject requests.
  - Append comments to requests.
- **Admin**:
  - Approve or reject requests.
  - Append comments to requests.

##### **Workflow**
- **Approval Flow**: Editor → Reviewer → Admin.
